summary.text: Take \(n=p=2\). Directly, the numerator and denominator defining \(a(4)\) are both \(96\), so \(a(4)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))=0\), while the proposed sum is \(\lfloor2/2\rfloor+\lfloor1/2\rfloor+0+\cdots=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{k=1}^{N}\gcd(j,k)}
{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{N}\bigl(\lfloor N/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k}
\]
and let \(b(m)=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\). The conjecture asserts that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
 =\sum_{i\ge 0}b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right)
 =\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
We disprove this by taking
\[
n=2,\qquad p=2.
\]
These choices satisfy the hypotheses: \(n>0\), and \(p=2\) is prime. Since \(np=4\), we first compute \(a(4)\).

The numerator is
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{4}\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(j,k).
\]
For each fixed \(j\), the four factors are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc|c}
 j & \gcd(j,1)&\gcd(j,2)&\gcd(j,3)&\gcd(j,4)&
 \prod_{k=1}^4\gcd(j,k)\\ \hline
 1&1&1&1&1&1\\
 2&1&2&1&2&4\\
 3&1&1&3&1&3\\
 4&1&2&1&4&8
\end{array}
\]
Consequently the complete numerator is
\[
1\cdot4\cdot3\cdot8=96.
\]

The denominator is
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\bigl(\lfloor4/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k.
\]
Its four factors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1:&\quad (\lfloor4/1\rfloor!)^1=(4!)^1=24,\\
k=2:&\quad (\lfloor4/2\rfloor!)^2=(2!)^2=2^2=4,\\
k=3:&\quad (\lfloor4/3\rfloor!)^3=(1!)^3=1,\\
k=4:&\quad (\lfloor4/4\rfloor!)^4=(1!)^4=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the denominator is also
\[
24\cdot4\cdot1\cdot1=96.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(4)=\frac{96}{96}=1.
\]
Therefore the left-hand side of the conjectured identity is
\[
\operatorname{ord}_2(a(2\cdot2))=\operatorname{ord}_2(1)=0,
\]
because no positive power of \(2\) divides \(1\).

It remains to evaluate the conjectured right-hand side. For \(n=p=2\), it is
\[
\sum_{i\ge0}b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
We divide the indices into the three relevant cases.

For \(i=0\), since \(2^0=1\),
\[
b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^0}\right\rfloor\right)
=b(2)=\left\lfloor\frac22\right\rfloor=1.
\]

For \(i=1\),
\[
b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^1}\right\rfloor\right)
=b(1)=\left\lfloor\frac12\right\rfloor=0.
\]

Finally, if \(i\ge2\), then
\[
2^i\ge2^2=4>2.
\]
Hence \(\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor=0\), and therefore
\[
b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor\right)=b(0)=0.
\]
Thus every term from index \(2\) onward vanishes, and the infinite sum reduces to
\[
1+0+0+\cdots=1.
\]

For the admissible pair \((n,p)=(2,2)\), the conjecture would therefore require
\[
0=\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))
 =\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
 =1,
\]
which is impossible. Hence the claimed identity does not hold for every positive integer \(n\) and prime \(p\), so conjecture D is false.
